title: Quogue
summary: Quogue is recorded as a village in western Southampton on Quantuck Bay. The name is a shortened form of Quaquanantuck, the older name for the salt meadows and land in this section.
introduction_content: Quogue is part of a continuing Shinnecock landscape, not simply a resort village with an old name. The shortened place name connects the present community to the wider Quaquanantuck geography and to contested colonial land transactions. Tooker, pp. 207–208
history_content:
The Quogue Historical Society describes the May 12, 1659 Ogden transaction while also noting reserved Native uses including hunting, fishing, fowling and gathering berries. Reading those provisions alongside the sale language changes the story: a colonial deed did not mean that Native people or their relationships with this land vanished. Quogue history and Shinnecock land

Shinnecock family history continued in Quogue through Mary Nancy Lee Enos and her daughter Mathilda “Tillie” Enos Dent, who operated the Shinnecock Arms. Their story connects Native kinship with the village’s working and lodging history. Explore the museum and family history. The Enos family and Shinnecock Arms, Quogue
translation_content:
Quogue is not derived from the Narragansett word for round clam. It is treated here as a shortened form of Quaquanantuck, interpreted as a cove or estuary where the land or water quakes or trembles.

Why Place Names Matter

“Place names are links to the past, mirrors reflecting various scenarios and activities of the past.”

— Marcas Mac Coinnigh, Memory and Landscape (2026), Opening discussion

Quogue shows how a long Indigenous placename was shortened into the modern village name while still carrying the older meadow, bay, and purchase history of western Southampton.
preservation_content: Quogue shows how a long Indigenous placename was shortened into the modern village name while still carrying the older meadow, bay, and purchase history of western Southampton.
whereintheworld_content: This point locates present-day Quogue village for orientation. Earlier Quogue and Quaquanantuck references could cover a much wider tract, so the village marker is not a boundary of that historical purchase. Visit the linked Quogue Historical Society entry for a public place to explore local records and family histories. Tooker, pp. 207–208
